title: The Seeing-Nature Does Not Perish
author: Annotated by Mingde
excerpt: At that time King Prasenajit rose and addressed the Buddha: “In the past, before I received the admonitions of the Buddhas, I saw Katyayana and Vairatiputra, who all said that this body is annihilated after death, and called this nirvāṇa. inline.s: (The original text is excerpted from the Surangama Sutra.)
At that time King Prasenajit rose and addressed the Buddha: “In the past, before I received the admonitions of the Buddhas, I saw Katya
zhān
yana and Vairati
zhī

putra, who all said that this body is annihilated after death, and called this nirvāṇa. Although I have now met the Buddha, I still harbor doubt. How may this mind be revealed and realized to dwell in the ground of neither arising nor ceasing? Now the whole assembly, all those with outflows, all wish to hear.”

At this time King Prasenajit rose and addressed the Buddha: “In the past I had not received the teachings of the Buddhas. I saw the heretics Katyayana and Vairatiputra, who all said that this body is annihilated after death (this is the view that death is like a lamp going out), and called this nirvāṇa. Later, although I encountered the Buddha, to this day I still doubt whether there is nothing at all after death. How can it be explained and realized that this mind neither arises nor ceases? Now, in this assembly, all those who have not yet extinguished their afflictions (those with outflows) all long to hear.”

[To address] To state something from an inferior to a superior. [Annihilation] Nothing remains after death. [Outflows] “Outflow” is another name for affliction; having outflows means having afflictions.

The Buddha told the King: “Your body is here now. I ask you again: is this physical body of yours like vajra, everlasting and imperishable, or does it change and decay?” “World-Honored One, this present body of mine will in the end change and perish.” The Buddha said: “Great King, you have not yet perished—how do you know it will perish?” “World-Honored One, though this impermanent, decaying body of mine has not yet perished, I observe that before my eyes it passes away thought after thought, ever changing and never abiding, like fire turning to ash, gradually wasting away and perishing without cease. So I know for certain that this body will in the end perish completely.” The Buddha said: “So it is.”

The Buddha told the King: “Your body is right here. Now I ask you: is this physical body of yours like vajra, everlasting and imperishable, or is it changing and decaying?” King Prasenajit said: “World-Honored One, this present physical body of mine will in the end change and perish.” The Buddha said: “Great King, you have not yet perished—how do you know it will perish?” King Prasenajit said: “World-Honored One, though this impermanent, decaying body of mine has not yet perished, I observe that this body is decaying and wasting away at every moment, ceaselessly changing, like firewood gradually turning to ash and slowly wasting away without cease. Therefore I know for certain that this body will in the end perish completely.” The Buddha confirmed: “So it is.”
[Ever changing and never abiding] Ceaselessly changing into another appearance.
“Great King, your present age has already turned to old age. How does your countenance compare with the time when you were a child?” “World-Honored One, in my childhood my skin
còu
was moist and lustrous; when I grew to adulthood, my blood and vital energy were full. Now in my declining years, pressed by old age
mào
, my form and complexion are withered, my spirit dulled, my hair white, my face wrinkled, and
dài
I will not last long. How can I compare with the time when I was full of vigor?”

Great King, you have already grown old in years. How does your countenance compare with your childhood?” “World-Honored One, in my childhood my skin was moist and lustrous; when I grew to adulthood, my blood and vital energy were full. Now in my late years, growing ever more aged, my appearance is haggard, my spirit dulled, my hair white, my face wrinkled, and I will soon pass away. How can my present countenance compare with that of my childhood?”

The Buddha said to the King: “Your appearance surely has not aged all at once.” The King said: “World-Honored One, the change moves on in secret, and I truly do not perceive it; cold and heat pass in succession, and gradually I have come to this. Why? At twenty, though called youthful, my appearance was already older than at ten; at thirty, it had declined further from twenty; now at sixty-two, looking back on my fifties, I still seemed robust. World-Honored One, I see this secret shifting—although it leads to my decline, the passing changes I measure by periods of ten years. But if I were to reflect more subtly, the change is not merely by twelve-year or twenty-four-year cycles, but truly year by year; and not merely year by year, but month by month; and not merely month by month, but day by day. Pondering deeply and observing closely, in every instant, in every thought-moment, it does not cease. Therefore I know my body will in the end change and perish.”

The Buddha said to the King: “Your appearance surely has not aged suddenly, has it?” The King said: “World-Honored One, the change in appearance is hidden and unseen; I do not perceive it at all. Year after year I have gradually become what I am now. Why do I say so? At twenty, though called youthful, my appearance was already older than at ten; at thirty, it had declined further from twenty; now at sixty-two, looking back on how strong I was at fifty, it is still clear before my eyes. World-Honored One, I see this hidden change moving toward death, viewing it in periods of ten years. But if I were to reflect more subtly, how could the change be only by periods of ten or twenty years? It truly changes year by year; and not merely year by year, but month by month; and not merely month by month, but day by day. Pondering deeply and observing closely, this change, in every instant and in every thought-moment, never ceases. Therefore I know my body will in the end be annihilated.”

[One ji] The Year Star (Jupiter) completes one circuit in twelve years, so anciently twelve years was called one ji. [Observing closely] To examine and look carefully. [An instant (ksana)] A moment. This is the smallest unit of time in ancient India.
The Buddha told the King: “You see change moving on without cease, and so you realize that you will perish. Yet at the very time of perishing,
do you know that within your body there is that which does not perish
King Prasenajit joined his palms and addressed the Buddha: “I truly do not know.” The Buddha said:
“I will now show you the nature that neither arises nor ceases.
Great King, at what age did you see the water of the Ganges?” The King said: “When I was three, my kind mother carried me to pay homage to the elder god Jiva
qí

deva, and passing by this river I then knew it was the water of the Ganges.” The Buddha said: “Great King, as you have said, at twenty you had declined from ten, and so on up to sixty—changing day by day, month by month, year by year, thought by thought. Then when you saw this river at three, by the time you reached thirteen, how was its water?” The King said: “As at three, it was exactly the same, without difference; and even now at sixty-two, it is still without difference.”

The Buddha told the King: “You see change passing on without cease, and so you realize that you will be annihilated. At the very time of this annihilation, do you know that within your body there is that which does not perish?” King Prasenajit joined his palms and addressed the Buddha: “I truly do not know.” The Buddha said: “I will now reveal to you the non-arising, non-ceasing essence (the nature) within the body. Great King, at what age did you see the water of the Ganges?” The King said: “When I was three, my kind mother carried me to pay homage to the Jiva deva (the deity of long life), and passing by this river I then knew it was the water of the Ganges.” The Buddha said: “Great King, as you have said, at twenty you were older than at ten, and so on, aging year by year until sixty—changing day by day, month by month, year by year, and at every moment. Then the seeing with which you saw this river at three, compared with the seeing with which you saw this river at thirteen—how is it?” The King said: “The seeing with which I saw the river at thirteen is exactly as it was at three, without any change; and even now at sixty-two, it is still without change.”
[To reveal] To make clear what was originally hard to know. For example: to reveal an objective law. [Nature] Means essence.

The Buddha said: “You now lament your white hair and wrinkled face; your face must be more wrinkled than in childhood. Then the seeing with which you now regard the Ganges, and the seeing with which you regarded it as a child—is there a difference of childhood and old age?” The King said: “No, World-Honored One.” The Buddha said: “Great King, though your face is wrinkled, the essence of this seeing has never wrinkled. What wrinkles changes; what does not wrinkle does not change. What changes will perish,
but that which does not change is originally free of arising and ceasing—how could it undergo your birth and death?
And yet you still cite those such as Maskari, all saying that this body is wholly annihilated after death.”

The Buddha said: “You now lament your white hair and wrinkled face; the wrinkles on your face now must be more numerous than in childhood. Then the seeing with which you now regard the Ganges, and the seeing with which you regarded it as a child in former days—is there a difference of old and young?” The King said: “No, World-Honored One.” The Buddha said: “Great King, though your face is covered with wrinkles, this seeing-nature has never had wrinkles (a metaphor for the seeing-nature not having aged with the passing of time). What wrinkles changes; what does not wrinkle does not change. What changes will perish, but that which does not change is originally free of arising and ceasing—how could it have birth and death? And yet you still cite the words of heretics such as Maskari, saying that this body is wholly annihilated after death.”
[Old age (
mào
)] Advanced in years.

When the King heard these words, he believed and knew that after death he would leave this life and go on to another life. With the whole assembly, he leaped for joy, having attained what he had never had before.

Having heard the World-Honored One’s instruction, King Prasenajit was suddenly and greatly awakened, and knew for certain that within the body there is an imperishable essence, and that after death he would be reborn (go on to another life). With the whole assembly, he leaped for joy, having attained what he had never had before.

[Leaving this life and going on to another life] After leaving this life, to go on to another life. That is, the imperishable essence within the body, when this present life comes to an end, will leave this body (leaving this life) to begin the next life (going on to another life). It is a pity that ordinary people always take this physical body to be themselves, and so they are boundlessly terrified of aging and death.
